newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean workers defy "slavery" law.
newsitem.headline: South Korean workers defy "slavery" law.

text.p: Accusing the government of wanting to turn workers into slaves, South Korean unions lashed out on Saturday at a new labour law. But a top government politician dismissed their fears as a "big misunderstanding".
"The new law will turn us workers into slaves," said Chun Jong-il, a Kia Motors worker who left his metal pressing machine to join strikes sparked by passage of the law on Thursday.
"Parliament members are not politicians -- they're thieves," he said as he took part in a protest rally by workers in a Seoul park that ended in pitched battles with police.
Ruling New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo tried to assure unions the law would benefit both workers and management.
"This is all a big misunderstanding," he said. "We struggled to write a law that would protect workers' rights and gain management flexibility for competitiveness."
He said the labour law needed to be overhauled to meet the demands of "globalisation and an information-driven society".
The government argues that rigid work practices that virtually guaranteed jobs for life have raised costs and hampered South Korea's international competitiveness.
Under the new law, companies can lay off surplus workers, hire temporary staff and replace strikers.
Lee's soothing words failed to assuage the anger of workers who see their livelihoods threatened. At Saturday's rally they demanded President Kim Young-sam resign.
Chun said losses caused by the strikes were the price that had to be paid for worker security. "It's an investment for my children, an investment for the future," he said.
Under a forest of banners and flags, workers wearing blue and red headbands chanted slogans and sang union songs.
"Overthrow the democracy-killing Kim Young-sam government," they shouted. Witnesses said 6,000 workers filled the park.
"Democracy is dead. I urge you to wear black ribbons to mourn its death," said union leader Chun Sae-young, bellowing through a microphone to the cheering crowds.
"We had expectations for Kim Young-sam. He was an opposition member, but he has stabbed us in the back," Chun said. Kim was once South Korea's most prominent dissident.

"The government is using workers as a tool to achieve their political goals," said construction worker Kim Young-gul, who shaved his head in protest. "They will use the current situation to rouse the conservative public for next year's election."
South Korea holds presidential polls next December, and although President Kim cannot run for a second term, he is expected to endorse a successor.
The peaceful rally turned violent when protesters tried to march through a main street and riot police beat them back with volleys of tear gas.

"We will respond to force with force," said Kim Young-dae, vice-president of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, the sponsorer of the rally. "We will carry out the strikes as planned and no rallies will be cancelled."
"We have been holding peaceful rallies and the government has brought in the riot police," said Kim who said he could not rule out the possibilty of more violent demonstrations.
